title: Tiny specks jiggling in water helped prove that atoms are real

cover.alt: A golden-brown microscope view crowded with small dark specks and pale particles suspended in liquid.

body: Under a microscope, specks suspended in water never settle down: they jitter and wander at random, however long you watch. Botanist Robert Brown saw this in 1827 in particles from pollen grains, but could not explain it. In 1905 Albert Einstein showed it is what you would expect if the water is made of molecules that keep hitting each speck, a few more on one side than the other at any instant. Jean Perrin's careful experiments in 1908 matched Einstein's predictions, helping to settle the long debate over whether atoms exist.

slides.alt: A microscope view of many small dark and pale particles in a golden liquid. They jiggle on the spot and drift a little in random directions, some blurring as they move in and out of focus.
slides.caption: Under a microscope, tiny particles suspended in a liquid jiggle and drift at random, nudged by molecules far too small to see. Time-lapse footage.
slides.credit: V. L. Fedorov · CC BY-SA 4.0 · excerpt

slides.prompt: Botanist Robert Brown first saw the jiggling in particles from pollen, so it might have been life. How did he rule that out?
slides.answer: Specks of glass and rock dust did it too
slides.detail: He repeated the experiment with inorganic particles, which jiggled just the same, so the cause had to be physical, not biological.

slides.heading: Why a speck never sits still

Each instant, one side gets a few more hits
The speck lurches one way, then another

events.text: Robert Brown sees particles from pollen jiggling in water
Einstein explains the motion as molecules hitting the particles
Jean Perrin's experiments confirm Einstein's predictions
Perrin wins the Nobel Prize in Physics

slides.question: Einstein's theory of the jiggling let scientists work out what?
slides.explanation: By linking how quickly the specks spread out to the molecules hitting them, it gave the size of atoms and how many atoms there are in a mole.
